questions.prompt: What defines the Singleton design pattern in Swift?

options.text: A class that instantiates new objects whenever a method is called
options.explanation: This describes a Factory pattern rather than a Singleton.

options.text: A class that restricts instantiation to a single shared instance throughout the app lifecycle
options.explanation: A singleton provides a single shared instance and prevents external instantiation.

options.text: A struct that can never be modified once declared
options.explanation: Immutable structs are value types, not singletons.

options.text: A protocol that can only be adopted by classes
options.explanation: AnyObject protocols restrict conformance, but do not create singletons.

questions.prompt: How does Swift make sure static let properties in a singleton are created safely across threads?

options.text: By executing all property initializers on background dispatch queues
options.explanation: Swift static initialization does not spawn background dispatch queues.

options.text: By generating C++ mutex locks around every method call
options.explanation: Method calls are not wrapped in C++ mutex locks.

options.text: By using lazy atomic initialization built into the Swift runtime
options.explanation: The Swift runtime initializes static let variables lazily with built-in atomic guarantees (similar to dispatch_once).

options.text: By disabling multi-core execution on the device
options.explanation: The Swift runtime does not alter device hardware settings.

questions.prompt: Which Apple system class is a canonical example of a Singleton?

options.explanation: UIView is instantiated many times across a view hierarchy.
String is a standard Swift value type.
URLRequest is a value type created for individual network calls.
FileManager.default provides a shared singleton instance representing the file system.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the Factory design pattern?

options.text: Centralizing object creation logic and returning protocol abstractions to callers
options.explanation: A factory instantiates concrete objects based on inputs and returns abstract types.

options.text: Persisting model entities directly to Core Data
options.explanation: Persistence is handled by database frameworks, not the Factory pattern.

options.text: Preventing any new instances from being created in memory
options.explanation: Factories create instances rather than preventing their creation.

options.text: Converting JSON data into Swift structs automatically
options.explanation: JSON decoding is performed by Codable.

questions.prompt: Which design pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface expected by clients?

options.explanation: The Singleton pattern restricts instance creation.
The Adapter pattern wraps an incompatible interface and translates it to match a target protocol.
The Observer pattern manages event broadcasting to subscribers.
The Builder pattern constructs complex objects step by step.

questions.prompt: Why should a singleton class declare a private init()?

options.text: To hide all class methods from unit test targets
options.explanation: Private initializers hide the constructor, not other class methods.

options.text: To tell the compiler to store the instance on the stack
options.explanation: Classes are always reference types allocated on the heap.

options.text: To prevent external callers from creating independent instances
options.explanation: A private initializer ensures only the single shared instance can ever be created.

options.text: To speed up method dispatch to static inline speeds
options.explanation: Access levels do not convert dynamic class dispatch to static inline calls.

questions.prompt: In Swift 6 mode, why does a singleton class with mutable variables require @MainActor or concurrency isolation?

options.explanation: Swift 6 supports classes with strict concurrency rules.

options.text: Because singletons cannot be referenced in SwiftUI
options.explanation: Singletons can be referenced across SwiftUI views.

options.text: Because static variables are stored in read-only binary pages
options.explanation: Static properties are stored in mutable global memory.

options.text: To prevent data races caused by concurrent access to global mutable state
options.explanation: Global shared mutable state without actor isolation or synchronization causes compiler errors in Swift 6.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an Adapter pattern and a Facade pattern?

options.text: Adapter translates one interface to another, while Facade provides a simplified interface over a complex subsystem
options.explanation: Adapter bridges two specific interfaces, whereas Facade simplifies access to multiple subsystem components.

options.text: Adapter is creational, while Facade is behavioral
options.explanation: Both Adapter and Facade are Structural design patterns.

options.text: Adapter is only used in UIKit, while Facade is exclusive to SwiftUI
options.explanation: Both patterns are universal architectural patterns across all platforms.

options.text: Facade requires subclassing, while Adapter only works with enums
options.explanation: Neither pattern requires subclassing or enums.

questions.prompt: Why can singletons cause test pollution in an automated test suite?

options.text: Because singletons crash the Xcode test runner executable
options.explanation: Singletons compile and run normally in test runners.

options.text: Because mutable state altered by one test persists and affects subsequent tests
options.explanation: Tests run in undefined order; mutating shared singleton state causes flaky, order-dependent failures.

options.text: Because test runners execute without access to static properties
options.explanation: Static properties are fully accessible in test environments.

options.text: Because singletons cannot be imported into unit test files
options.explanation: Test files can import any module using @testable import.

questions.prompt: How can an engineering team make a singleton-based service testable with mocks?

options.text: By deleting the private initializer so any file can recreate it
options.explanation: Removing private init breaks the singleton contract without improving architecture.

options.text: By converting the singleton class into an Objective-C category
options.explanation: Categories do not solve dependency injection or test mocking.

options.text: By conforming the singleton to a protocol and injecting it through initializers
options.explanation: Declaring a protocol allows unit tests to inject mock objects while production callers use the default shared instance.

options.text: By declaring all properties as implicitly unwrapped optionals
options.explanation: Implicitly unwrapped optionals increase crash risk and do not help test mocking.

questions.prompt: Why is treating a singleton as a global storage bag an anti-pattern?

options.text: Because Swift garbage collection cannot track global variables
options.explanation: Swift uses ARC, not garbage collection, and tracks static variables properly.

options.text: Because iOS terminates apps that allocate more than one global variable
options.explanation: iOS does not terminate apps for allocating global variables.

options.text: Because global variables cannot store strings or integers
options.explanation: Global variables can store any Swift type.

options.text: Because it creates hidden dependencies and unpredictable cross-module coupling
options.explanation: When any class can read and write shared data anywhere, tracking bugs and isolating components becomes extremely difficult.

questions.prompt: What is the primary architectural purpose of the Strategy pattern in iOS?

options.text: Forcing all screens to inherit from a single base view controller
options.explanation: Base classes create rigid inheritance hierarchies, the opposite of the Strategy pattern.

options.text: Defining interchangeable algorithms conforming to a protocol that can be swapped at runtime
options.explanation: Strategy encapsulates distinct algorithms (e.g. sorting, caching, validation) behind a protocol.

options.text: Preventing any network requests during unit tests
options.explanation: Strategy allows swapping network strategies, but its purpose is broader than test prevention.

options.text: Converting class methods into static inline functions
options.explanation: Strategy is an object-oriented behavioral pattern, not a compiler optimization.

The Builder pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation.
